name: Malay
variety: Standard Malay. The segmental description follows the Standard Malay of Brunei (Clynes & Deterding 2011) with the differences of the Peninsular Malaysian standard based on Johor-Riau speech (the 'schwa variety'), which is the variety eSpeak NG follows
sources: Clynes, Adrian & Deterding, David (2011). Standard Malay (Brunei). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(2), 259-268.
Teoh, Boon Seong (1994). The Sound System of Malay Revisited. Kuala Lumpur: Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka.
Yunus Maris (1980). The Malay Sound System. Kuala Lumpur: Fajar Bakti.
Zuraidah Mohd Don, Knowles, Gerry & Yong, Janet (2008). How words can be misleading: a study of syllable timing and 'stress' in Malay. The Linguistics Journal 3(2).

Grabe, Esther & Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In C. Gussenhoven & N. Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7, 515-546. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Deterding, David (2011). Measurements of the rhythm of Malay. Proceedings of the 17th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Hong Kong, 576-579.
Soderberg, Craig D. & Olson, Kenneth S. (2008). Indonesian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 38(2), 209-213.
contrasts: six vowels including schwa; the spelling writes both /e/ and /ə/ as e
voiced versus voiceless stops and affricates at four places
four nasals m n ɲ ŋ
high and mid vowels contrast fully only in the penultimate syllable (bila versus bela, dua versus doa)
no vowel or consonant length, no tone, no lexical stress
f, v, z, ʃ, x occur only in loanwords; the glottal stop is marginal
allophony: word-final /a/ is [ə] in the Peninsular schwa variety (saya, apa, kita) and [a] in Brunei, Sabah, Sarawak, the north of the Peninsula and in the official 'baku' pronunciation
final /k/ is a glottal stop in Peninsular Malay; in Brunei it is an unreleased velar or uvular stop
voiceless stops are unaspirated, and unreleased in codas; newsreaders in Brunei aspirate them under English influence
/i u/ are lowered and centralised to [ɪ ʊ], or as far as [e o], in final closed syllables (bilik, burung); /e o/ are never raised
final /r/ is silent in the Peninsular schwa variety and pronounced as a trill or tap elsewhere
/r/ varies between trill and tap; the trill is more emphatic
/t/ is dental in many varieties, alveolar in Brunei
schwa is never prominent and is often dropped (semakin with [sm], bertiup with [br])
/u i/ before another vowel may become glides in fast speech (kuat as [kwat], siapa as [sjapa])
a glottal stop may separate vowels across a morpheme boundary (dianggap, mengenai) and appears in some Arabic loans (saat)
loan fricatives are replaced in colloquial speech: f by p, v by b, z by dʒ or s, ʃ by s, x by h or k
syllable_structure: (C)V(C); initial clusters only through loss of schwa or in loanwords
phonotactics: more than nine tenths of native roots have two syllables
a final consonant of a root is any consonant except the palatals tʃ dʒ ɲ and the voiced stops
a coda inside a root is a nasal homorganic with the next consonant, or r
the vowels i u e o of the last two syllables of a root agree in height (giling, burung, boleh); schwa does not occur in final syllables nor directly before another vowel
only i, u, a occur in final open syllables
ai, au, oi occur only at the end of a root and may be analysed as vowel plus glide /aj aw oj/; elsewhere adjacent vowels are separate syllables

stress.rule: Older descriptions give penultimate stress that skips schwa; acoustic studies find no word stress, only a prominence on the last word of a phrase.
stress.cues: a rise and fall in pitch over the penultimate and final syllables of the phrase; the final vowel is often lengthened; when the penultimate vowel is schwa the movement is confined to the final syllable

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: only schwa is short and may be dropped
rhythm.notes: Deterding (2011) measured a syllable-based vowel PVI of 40.9 for Brunei Malay readings of the North Wind passage against 59.9 for British English, using his own variant of the index, so the figure cannot be compared directly with the nPVI below.

npvi_v.source: Grabe & Low 2002 (one speaker; raw consonantal rPVI 63.3)

length.notes: No length contrasts; phrase-final vowels are phonetically lengthened.

intonation.declarative: rise and fall over the last two syllables of each phrase, ending low at the end of the utterance
intonation.yes_no_question: commonly described as a final rise on the last syllable when no question particle is used; the clitic -kah marks questions without the need for a rise
intonation.wh_question: not described in detail in the sources consulted
intonation.continuation: a rise on the final syllable of a non-final phrase, giving an impression of final stress
intonation.accent_shape: rise and fall starting on the penultimate syllable of the phrase-final word
intonation.notes: After Clynes & Deterding (2011) and Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong (2008).

phonation: unreleased final stops; glottal stop for final k in Peninsular Malay

problems: the letter e is still ambiguous between /e/ and /ə/; rules and a long exception list catch many words, the rest are guessed
ai and au are made diphthongs in closed syllables too, where the standard has two syllables (baik, laut, daun come out as one syllable)
final r is pronounced, although final a is made schwa as in the Johor-Riau based standard, where final r is silent; the result mixes two pronunciation norms
fixed penultimate stress marked by length and loudness, against the phrase-level prominence described in the literature
final stops other than k are released
good: final a becomes schwa and final k a glottal stop, as in Peninsular Malaysian speech
i and u are lowered in final closed syllables (kecil, putih, puluh)
reduced intonation range set in the voice file (intonation 3)

notes: In the one spectrogram measured by Clynes & Deterding (2011) an aspirated /k/ of their newsreader had 47 ms of aspiration; this is not typical of unaspirated Malay stops, so no voice onset time block is given.
